lessons.title: Trophic levels in an ecosystem
lessons.summary: Number the trophic levels of a food chain, draw pyramids of biomass to scale, find out where the biomass goes at each step, and calculate how efficiently it is passed from one level to the next.
objectives: I can describe the trophic levels in a food chain and number them from producer to apex predator.
I can explain the role of decomposers in an ecosystem.
I can construct and interpret a pyramid of biomass drawn to scale.
I can explain why only a small proportion of biomass is transferred from one trophic level to the next.
I can calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer between trophic levels.

activities.title: Trophic levels
activities.content:
## Numbering the food chain

Each feeding position in a food chain is called a **trophic level** (*trophic* just means "feeding"). Trophic levels are **numbered from the bottom up**, starting with the producers:

| Level | Name | What they do | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Producers** | plants and algae that make their own food (glucose) by **photosynthesis** | oak tree, grass, phytoplankton |
| **2** | **Primary consumers** | herbivores that eat producers | caterpillar, rabbit, zooplankton |
| **3** | **Secondary consumers** | carnivores that eat herbivores | blue tit, stoat, small fish |
| **4** | **Tertiary consumers** | carnivores that eat other carnivores | sparrowhawk, fox, tuna |

The consumer at the very top of a chain, with **no predators of its own**, is the **apex predator**.

```
grass (1)  ->  grasshopper (2)  ->  frog (3)  ->  heron (4, apex predator)
```

One organism can sit at different levels in different chains: a fox eating a rabbit is at level 3, but a fox eating a stoat that ate a rabbit is at level 4.

**Decomposers** – bacteria and fungi – do not appear as a numbered level, but they are vital. They **secrete enzymes** onto dead plants, animals and waste, digest the material outside their bodies, and absorb the small soluble molecules that result. In doing so they return mineral ions to the soil and carbon dioxide to the air, keeping the ecosystem's nutrients cycling.

question.text: In the food chain *seaweed → periwinkle (sea snail) → crab → seagull*, match each organism to its trophic level.
question.hint: Producers are level 1; count upwards along the arrows.
question.explanation: Seaweed is the producer (level 1), the periwinkle eats it (level 2), the crab eats the periwinkle (level 3) and the seagull eats the crab (level 4).

activities.title: Pyramids of biomass
activities.content:
## Weighing each level

**Biomass** is the mass of living material. A **pyramid of biomass** shows the **total dry mass** of all the organisms at each trophic level in a food chain, at one moment in time.

Rules for drawing one:

- **Trophic level 1 (producers) goes at the bottom**, with level 2 above it, and so on.
- Each bar is drawn **to scale** – its width represents the biomass at that level (units are usually g/m² or kg/m²).
- The bars are centred, so the shape is symmetrical.

```
            [ herons  2 ]
         [   frogs   35   ]
     [   grasshoppers  200   ]
[        grass       1500          ]
```

Biomass **decreases** at every step up the chain, so pyramids of biomass are almost always pyramid-shaped (unlike pyramids of *numbers*, which can be odd shapes when one big tree feeds thousands of insects).

**Why dry mass?** Water content varies hugely between organisms and over time, so biologists dry the samples and weigh what is left. In practice that means killing the organisms, so biomass is usually estimated from small samples rather than measured for a whole habitat.

The pyramid is a snapshot of *how much living material* there is at each level – the next section explains why each level holds so much less than the one below.

activities.title: Worked example: drawing a pyramid to scale
activities.content:
**A pond food chain has these biomass values: pondweed 800 g/m², water snails 90 g/m², sticklebacks 12 g/m², perch 2 g/m². Draw a pyramid of biomass.**

**Step 1 – choose a scale.** The largest value is 800, so let 1 cm represent 100 g/m². (Some students use 10 g/m² per mm, which is the same thing.)

**Step 2 – work out each bar width.**

| Level | Organism | Biomass (g/m²) | Width at 1 cm : 100 g/m² |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | pondweed | 800 | 8.0 cm |
| 2 | water snails | 90 | 0.9 cm |
| 3 | sticklebacks | 12 | 0.12 cm |
| 4 | perch | 2 | 0.02 cm |

**Step 3 – draw.** Producers at the bottom, all bars the same height, each bar centred on the one below.

**Step 4 – label** each bar with the organism *and* the biomass value, and state the scale.

**Watch out:** the top bars come out very thin. That is correct – it *is* the point of the pyramid. Do not widen them to make them look nicer, but do label them clearly so the examiner can see they are there.

**Follow-up question you might be asked:** *How many times greater is the biomass of pondweed than of perch?* 800 ÷ 2 = **400 times**.

question.text: Which statement about a pyramid of biomass is correct?
question.hint: Think about which organisms go at the bottom and what the width of each bar means.
question.explanation: Producers form the bottom bar and each bar's width is proportional to the biomass at that level. Biomass decreases up the pyramid, and it is measured as dry mass.

options.text: The producers form the bottom bar and each bar is drawn to scale
The apex predator forms the bottom bar because it is the largest animal
options.feedback: Producers always go at the bottom, whatever their size.

options.text: The bars show the number of organisms at each level
options.feedback: That is a pyramid of numbers.

options.text: Biomass increases as you move up the pyramid

activities.title: Where the biomass goes
activities.content:
## Losses at every step

Only a small fraction of the biomass at one trophic level ends up as biomass in the next. Two figures to learn:

- Producers convert only about **1 %** of the light energy that falls on them into biomass by photosynthesis. The rest is reflected, passes through the leaf, or is the wrong wavelength.
- Roughly **10 %** of the biomass at one trophic level is passed on to the next level. About **90 %** is lost.

**Why is so much lost between consumers?**

1. **Not everything is eaten.** Roots, bark, bones, fur and shells are often left behind.
2. **Not everything eaten is absorbed.** Some material cannot be digested and is egested as **faeces**.
3. **Some absorbed material is lost as waste.** Excess protein is broken down and lost as **urea** in urine; carbon dioxide and water leave through breathing.
4. **Much of the absorbed glucose is used in respiration** to release energy for **movement** and, in mammals and birds, for **keeping warm**. That energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat and is not stored as biomass.

Only the material that is turned into new cells – growth, or the offspring produced – counts as biomass available to the next level.

**Why food chains are short**

Because 90 % is lost at each step, after four or five levels there is too little biomass left to support another population of predators. That is why food chains rarely have more than five links, and why apex predators are relatively rare.

question.text: A rabbit eats grass. Which of the following explain why not all the biomass in the grass becomes biomass in the rabbit? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about what leaves the rabbit's body and what it uses energy for.
question.explanation: Some of the grass is indigestible and leaves as faeces, and much of the glucose absorbed is used in respiration for movement and warmth rather than for growth. Rabbits do not photosynthesise, and they gain (not lose) biomass by growing.

options.text: Some grass cannot be digested and is egested as faeces
Much of the absorbed glucose is used in respiration for movement and keeping warm
The rabbit uses some of the biomass for photosynthesis
The rabbit loses biomass every time it grows
options.feedback: Growth is how biomass is gained.

activities.title: Calculating efficiency of transfer
activities.content:
## Putting a number on it

The **efficiency of biomass transfer** between two trophic levels is:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{biomass transferred to the next level}}{\text{biomass available at the previous level}} \times 100\%$$

So if 500 kg of grass supports 40 kg of rabbits, the efficiency of transfer from level 1 to level 2 is 40 ÷ 500 × 100 = **8 %**.

**Tips for the calculation**

- Make sure both biomass values are in the **same unit** before dividing (convert kg to g or g to kg if the question mixes them).
- The answer is a percentage and is normally **below 10 %**. If you get 90 % or 500 %, you have probably divided the wrong way round.
- Sometimes the question gives you the energy content instead of the mass. The method is exactly the same: energy in the next level ÷ energy in the previous level × 100.
- You may also be asked to find the **biomass lost**: available − transferred.

**Working backwards**

If a question tells you the efficiency and the biomass of one level, rearrange the formula. With 10 % efficiency, a level holding 300 g/m² can support 300 × 10 ÷ 100 = **30 g/m²** at the next level; and a level holding 30 g/m² must have been fed by 30 ÷ 0.10 = **300 g/m²** below it.

activities.title: Worked example: efficiency between three levels
activities.content:
**In a grassland, the biomass of the producers is 6400 kg. The primary consumers (insects) have a biomass of 640 kg, and the secondary consumers (birds) have a biomass of 48 kg.**

**(a) Calculate the efficiency of transfer from producers to primary consumers.**

efficiency = 640 ÷ 6400 × 100 = **10 %**

**(b) Calculate the efficiency of transfer from primary to secondary consumers.**

efficiency = 48 ÷ 640 × 100 = **7.5 %**

**(c) Suggest why the transfer in (b) is less efficient than in (a).**

The birds are **warm-blooded**, so they use a large proportion of the biomass they absorb in respiration to **maintain their body temperature**, leaving less for growth. Insects do not spend energy keeping warm. Birds also **move around more** searching for food.

**(d) Calculate the mass of biomass lost between the primary and secondary consumers.**

640 − 48 = **592 kg**, lost as faeces, urea, and heat from respiration.

**Checking your answers:** both efficiencies are under 10 %, which is what we expect, and the losses are large, which matches the idea that pyramids of biomass narrow sharply at each level.

question.text: In a lake, phytoplankton have a biomass of 2500 kg. The zooplankton that feed on them have a biomass of 225 kg. Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer from phytoplankton to zooplankton. Give your answer as a percentage.
question.hint: Divide the biomass at the higher level by the biomass at the lower level, then multiply by 100.

question.text: Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels.
question.hint: Think about how much biomass reaches each level compared with the one below.
question.explanation: About 90 % of the biomass is lost at each transfer, so after several levels there is very little biomass left. There would not be enough to support a population of organisms at a sixth level.

markScheme.criterion: Biomass / energy is lost at each level (only about 10 % passed on)
Eventually not enough biomass to support another level / population

question.text:
The table shows the biomass at each trophic level of a food chain in a meadow.

| Trophic level | Organism | Biomass (g/m²) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | grass | 1200 |
| 2 | voles | 96 |
| 3 | owls | 6 |

(a) Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer from the voles to the owls. **(2 marks)**

(b) Explain **two** reasons why most of the biomass in the voles is not transferred to the owls. **(2 marks)**

(c) Explain why the owls are described as the apex predator in this food chain. **(1 mark)**
question.hint: Efficiency = next level ÷ previous level × 100. For (b), think about faeces, urea and respiration.
question.explanation: (a) 6 ÷ 96 × 100 = 6.25 %. (b) Some parts of the vole (bones, fur) are not digested and are egested as faeces; much of what is absorbed is used in respiration to release energy for movement and keeping warm, and this energy is lost as heat; some is lost as urea in urine. (c) Owls have no predators of their own, so they are at the top of the chain.

markScheme.criterion: Some material not digested / lost as faeces (or not all of the vole is eaten)
Biomass used in respiration for movement / keeping warm, lost as heat (or lost as urea)
Owls have no predators / nothing eats them

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Trophic levels** are numbered from the bottom: **1 producers**, **2 primary consumers**, **3 secondary consumers**, **4 tertiary consumers**. The top consumer with no predators is the **apex predator**.
- **Decomposers** secrete enzymes to break down dead material and waste, recycling nutrients.
- A **pyramid of biomass** shows the dry mass at each level, drawn **to scale** with **producers at the bottom**. Biomass decreases at every level.
- Producers turn only about **1 %** of light energy into biomass; only about **10 %** of biomass passes from one level to the next.
- Losses: not all eaten; **faeces** (undigested), **urea**, and glucose used in **respiration** for movement and warmth (lost as heat).
- **Efficiency = biomass in next level ÷ biomass in previous level × 100 %**. Check units match and expect an answer below 10 %.
- Large losses at each step are why food chains are short.

practiceQuestions.text: Which trophic level do producers occupy?
practiceQuestions.hint: Trophic levels are numbered from the bottom of the food chain.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Producers are always trophic level 1 because every food chain starts with them.

options.text: Level 1
Level 2
Level 3
Level 4

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a pyramid of biomass always has the producers at the bottom.
practiceQuestions.hint: The bars are stacked in trophic level order.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Trophic level 1 (producers) forms the base, with consumers stacked above in order.

options.text: True
False

metadata.blanksText: Producers transfer only about ___ % of the light energy that falls on them into biomass. Approximately ___ % of the biomass at one trophic level is transferred to the next.

practiceQuestions.hint: Both numbers are small; the second is ten times the first.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Producers convert about 1 % of incident light energy into biomass; about 10 % of biomass is transferred between trophic levels.

practiceQuestions.text: What is the role of decomposers in an ecosystem?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what happens to dead leaves on a forest floor.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) secrete enzymes to break down dead organisms and waste, releasing nutrients back into the environment.

options.text: They break down dead organisms and waste, recycling nutrients
They make glucose by photosynthesis
They hunt and eat primary consumers
They store biomass so it is not lost

practiceQuestions.text: Arrange these organisms from trophic level 1 to trophic level 4.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start with the organism that photosynthesises.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Algae are producers (1); tadpoles eat algae (2); dragonfly nymphs eat tadpoles (3); kingfishers eat dragonfly nymphs (4).

practiceQuestions.text: Grass in a field has a biomass of 5000 kg. Assuming 10 % of biomass is transferred to the next level, what biomass of sheep could this grass support? Give your answer in kg.
The biomass of caterpillars in a wood is 180 kg and the biomass of the blue tits that eat them is 12.6 kg. Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer as a percentage.
Which of the following are ways in which biomass is lost from a food chain between trophic levels? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what leaves an animal's body.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Biomass is lost through respiration (energy transferred as heat), and through waste such as faeces and urea. Growth and reproduction are the ways biomass is retained and passed on.

options.text: Energy released in respiration is transferred to the surroundings as heat
Undigested material is lost as faeces
Biomass is stored when the organism grows
options.feedback: Growth keeps biomass in the chain.

options.text: Biomass passed on when the organism reproduces
options.feedback: Offspring are new biomass at the same level, not a loss.

practiceQuestions.text: A pyramid of biomass for a woodland has a very wide base representing a single oak tree, yet a pyramid of numbers for the same food chain would have a very narrow base. Explain the difference.
practiceQuestions.hint: One tree is one organism, but it has an enormous mass.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A pyramid of numbers counts individuals, and there is only one oak tree, so the base is narrow. A pyramid of biomass shows mass, and the single oak has a huge mass – far more than all the insects feeding on it – so the base is wide.

markScheme.criterion: Pyramid of numbers counts individuals; only one tree so base is narrow
Pyramid of biomass shows mass; the tree has a very large mass so base is wide

practiceQuestions.text:
A farmer keeps cattle in a barn heated to 20 °C rather than in an open field. She claims the cattle grow faster on the same amount of food.

(a) Explain why the farmer's claim is likely to be correct. **(2 marks)**

(b) The cattle are fed 4800 kg of hay and gain 360 kg of biomass. Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer. **(2 marks)**
practiceQuestions.hint: Warm animals use less energy in respiration to keep warm, leaving more for growth. Then divide 360 by 4800.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) In the warm barn the cattle lose less heat to the surroundings, so they use less of the biomass they absorb in respiration to maintain body temperature. They also move less in a barn. More of the food is therefore converted into growth (new biomass). (b) 360 ÷ 4800 × 100 = 7.5 %.

markScheme.criterion: Cattle use less energy / respire less to keep warm (or move less)
So more of the food biomass is used for growth / converted into biomass

practiceQuestions.text: Only about 1 % of the light energy reaching a field of wheat is converted into biomass by the plants. Give **three** reasons why the other 99 % is not converted into biomass.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what can happen to light when it hits a leaf, and about what the plant does with the glucose it makes.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Some light is reflected from the leaf surface; some passes straight through the leaves or misses them; some is of the wrong wavelength for chlorophyll to absorb; and some of the glucose made is used by the plant in respiration rather than being stored as biomass.

markScheme.criterion: Light is reflected from the leaves
Light passes through / misses the leaves, or is of the wrong wavelength / colour to be absorbed
Some glucose produced is used in respiration by the plant
